sections.title: It doesn't have to be in person

blocks.p: Have you ever felt calmer and more secure just by being around a specific person? You feel safer with that person because of something called co-regulation. This deep-rooted biological process plays a vital role in shaping your emotional and physiological states. From the calming effect of a loved one's presence to the subtle cues of safety we exchange with those around us, co-regulation is an essential part of being human, and of healing from trauma.

The Polyvagal Theory has numerous helpful pieces, like understanding our body's autonomic states, how we shift into and out of them, and how somebody gets stuck in trauma. Co-regulation is another key piece. It intertwines our neurobiological responses with our interpersonal relationships, so it helps explain how our biology connects to our relationships. And co-regulation might actually help you get unstuck.

Co-regulation refers to how our emotional and physiological states are influenced, and also stabilized, through interactions with others: safe others. When we interact with somebody who is in their safety state, that helps us access our own safety state. Basically, co-regulation helps us feel calmer and more connected when we're around somebody who's safe.

Co-regulation is a fundamental aspect of attachment and connection for us humans. It lies at the center of how we connect and how we empathize with those around us. And it's not just humans, but all mammals. We use some form of co-regulation within our species, human to human, and also between species, like human to dog. There really isn't much co-regulation at all between a human and a fish, or a lizard, or a bird. You might feel good around them, but that's different from co-regulation. I'll come back to why.

Co-regulation is deeply rooted in our autonomic nervous system. It's not just a behavior, like hugging or actively listening to someone who needs it. It might look like that on the outside, but really it's a neurobiological process that happens between two or more mammals. We'll stick with two.

The Polyvagal Theory teaches us that when somebody is in their safety state, their body is in a state of homeostasis, of balance, of optimal functioning. It uses its resources for health and growth and restoration. Co-regulation can help lead to that safety state, and all those benefits. For someone who's stuck in trauma, co-regulation can help them enter their ventral vagal safety pathways. In the therapeutic process, this is essential: therapists have to be co-regulators to help their clients access safety. But for those stuck in trauma, co-regulation is also a pretty big challenge to give and to receive. It's still potentially very helpful.
Let's look at the neurobiological foundations of co-regulation, just for a nerdy moment.
The Polyvagal Theory says we have three distinct states of the autonomic nervous system, responsible for three distinct bodily states:

ol: Safety, which brings calm, confidence, connection, happiness, and more.
Mobilization, which brings flight and fight, to evade or avoid danger, or to aggress upon it.
Immobilization, which we call shutdown. It pops up when we're in life threat, and it basically mimics death.

blocks.p: The state of our autonomic nervous system is constantly influenced by our interactions with the external world, and that includes the people in it. We directly impact each other's state. My voice impacts the state of whoever is listening to me. My eye contact, or my lack of it when I'm relying on my notes, impacts the state of whoever is watching.
So yes, you guessed it: positive interactions affect us positively. But what's happening underneath the interaction? Co-regulation is not the interaction. It's the biology underneath it.

The Polyvagal Theory hypothesizes that we have specific autonomic pathways responsible for calming our heart and optimizing our bodily functions when we're in that safety state. These are the ventral vagal pathways, and more specifically, the myelinated ventral vagal pathways, which are specific to mammals. That's why I said this is a mammalian thing.

When we have literal safety, our heartbeat calms down, and we can express to others externally that we're in our safety state. We do so with our face and our neck. We can tilt our head to the side with curiosity and playfulness. We smile with eye crinkles and upper cheek movement. These little facial and neck movements project safety to another. They say, "I'm a safe mammal. It's okay to lower your defenses."

We can also receive these cues from others, which helps us decrease our own defensive activation. So we as individuals can both project and receive safety, and that sets up what should ideally be a perpetual loop of giving and receiving safety cues with another.

When the safety cues are removed, it signals to the other mammal that there's danger present, whether literally or not. The body shifts state and orients to the danger, or the possible danger, in preparation for survival.

It doesn't have to be literal danger and survival. Think about when someone looks down at their phone while you're talking to them. You probably feel irritated. That irritation indicates you've shifted out of your safety state enough to notice. You're not getting up and running away or punching the person, I hope, but your state shifted enough for you to notice. Then when that person looks up, smiles at you, and apologizes, your system probably calms down, you return to a state of connection, and your irritation eases up.

Co-regulation through these nurturing social interactions can lead to numerous potential benefits, like reducing stress hormones, enabling higher brain functions, and enhancing feelings of well-being. Being in our safety state is just generally better for us. Like Dr. Porges says so often, this is where health and growth and restoration occur. Co-regulation can help us be in our safety state. So we very literally need each other.

Co-regulation is helping another person access their safety state through cues of safety. That means you first need access to your own safety state in order to offer cues of safety to someone else. That's self-regulation. You must be self-regulated in order to offer co-regulation.

Self-regulation is basically the ability to manage your own emotional state and behaviors. Underneath that, it's really the ability to access your own ventral vagal pathways, your own safety state. Self-regulation requires enough distress tolerance to deal with challenges. And distress tolerance requires a safety state strong enough to tolerate challenges without losing access to it. So to self-regulate, you need a lot of access to your ventral vagal pathways, and that's a big challenge for those in trauma recovery.
Co-regulation can be seen as a precursor to self-regulation. A child does not develop self-regulation without first receiving effective co-regulation from others, like a parent.

For someone in trauma recovery, the support and stability of co-regulating relationships can help build the strength of their safety state, which can eventually lead to more self-regulation. So co-regulation leads to self-regulation, which leads to co-regulation, which leads to self-regulation, and hopefully on and on. Once you're more self-regulated, you can offer co-regulation to others.

For trauma recovery, we kind of have to have a balance of co-regulation and self-regulation, and therapy does a really good job of this, or it should. Therapy offers co-regulation as a foundation for developing self-regulation. The predictable, safe connection with a therapist helps the client repeatedly access their safety state, even while discussing things that might be challenging. Embracing that therapeutic challenge, along with the co-regulation, helps strengthen their safety state.
Deb Dana put it this way when she was on the podcast:

q: We need enough experiences of safe co-regulation first and for many clients they've missed that. People have been dangerous and the therapist is taking on that role of being the first safe co-regulator in their life.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana: Book 2 and COVID-19 (episode 54)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a)

blocks.p: But even if you're not in therapy and you're doing your own self-healing work, connecting with other people through other avenues can still be helpful. It doesn't have to be in therapy.

On a practical level, giving and receiving co-regulation can be really difficult for people who are stuck in trauma. One member of my community said that even the word "connection" was too much for her. Expecting someone like that to strike up a conversation, or just go out and meet safe others, is probably going to be a lot. So co-regulation opportunities need to be practical for people in trauma recovery.

Co-regulation won't come from everyone. Realistically, not everybody in your life can co-regulate. Most may not be able to, not even your partner or your family. That's sad, but it might be true, even if they're trying really hard.
If that describes you:

ol: Identify who in your life is realistically co-regulative. There might be people who have shown they're safe, that they're co-regulative, and that they've earned a little more attention from you.
Increase your attention and your time with them. Not too much. Don't bombard them. Just make sure you reach out and try to connect.
Decrease your attention to those who aren't co-regulative. Decrease your vulnerability, especially, with people who haven't earned it.

blocks.p: My therapy clients often group their relationships, kind of ranking them. I know that might sound objective, maybe horrible. But it goes something like this: these are my core people. They deserve my time, and I'm allowing myself to be more exposed or vulnerable with them. Then there are people outside that core who are okay. We're friendly, but I'm not going to rely on them or ask of them more than I know they can give. And outside of that are acquaintances, where we chit-chat here and there.
If you can give your core people a bit more of yourself, and mindfully feel and experience their co-regulation cues, that can be really helpful. It helps nurture and build those relationships.

Co-regulation doesn't have to be for extended periods of time. It can be really small, brief moments, like sharing laughter with somebody. Even if you don't catch it in the moment and experience it mindfully, that's fine. Later on, remember what it was like and let yourself re-experience that moment of connection as much as you can. Notice where you feel that sense of connection, and try to relive it.

Co-regulation doesn't have to be with humans. Other mammals in your life are fine. Cats work really well, I think, but dogs are fantastic at this. The co-regulation pieces are all there: gentle touch through petting, sharing warmth by lying on or next to each other, making eye contact. There might even be some singing the two of you can do together. Dogs especially like to sing.

blocks.h3: It doesn't have to be in person

blocks.p: Virtual meetings are less than ideal, but they do work, even in therapy.

Therapy and coaching could be, or should be, great places for co-regulation, and so can mentoring. A professional relationship can provide reliable co-regulation. Or maybe it's your coworkers, who aren't your core group, but you exchange little co-regulating moments: smiles, laughter, vocal prosody. That's something.
I want to encourage you to create moments of co-regulation that you can tolerate. Not all moments with people are tolerable, obviously.

Who can you reach out to and express appreciation to? If you can do it in person, that's ideal. It allows for the full co-regulative, neurobiological, shared experience. But if reaching out through a text or a written letter is what's approachable for you, that's a good start. Maybe it's actually a great start. It's at least a feeling of connection, and it gets you going down the path toward actual, in-person, shared co-regulation.

Ask yourself what communities you can join. Are there clubs or activities? I've had therapy clients join biking groups, pottery, after-school clubs, and improv, or hang out with coworkers. All kinds of things that give them some level of connection that's approachable for them. One client let go of the pressure of trying to be around everybody at work, and instead focused on two people and really nurtured those relationships.
If you join your coworkers or friends for something, it might help to give yourself a limit: "This is how much co-regulation I can give and receive, and this is the time I'm leaving."
I don't know what that is for you. But ask yourself: what can you join? What can you be a part of that allows for some co-regulation?

Co-regulation is a necessity for us humans, and for all mammals. We need each other. We do not do well in solitude or isolation. We evolved with each other, and we evolved to connect with each other. Co-regulation leads to more safety state activation, better health outcomes, more emotional stability, homeostasis, and a whole bunch of other benefits.

Ideally, we build self-regulation on top of a healthy history of co-regulation throughout life. The reality is we don't always get that. Even though you should have gotten co-regulation to build self-regulation, you might not have, so you start where you're at, and that might be self-regulating. You can build the strength of your safety state. You can build your distress tolerance. You can build your connection with yourself, and even with others. That requires a dedicated, practical practice. Community members have told me that as they build their self-regulation, they're able to give and receive co-regulation with others.

Take a moment to reflect on your experiences with co-regulation, and consider how they've impacted your journey. How have your relationships influenced your healing process? Or have you lacked co-regulation from people you should have gotten it from? Reflect, or journal if you like.
Don't challenge yourself with this if it's too much for you. I don't want you going into any depth with re-traumatizing stories. Just keep it light and reflect.
